name: One vertex
why: ['colouring']. Small graphs are checked by solving your formula and reading a colour for each vertex from it.

name: Four, all joined
why: ['no colouring']: four vertices that all touch need four colours, so the formula must have no solution. Without the edge clauses it would have one.

name: An odd wheel
why: ['no colouring']: the rim, a cycle of 5, needs all three colours, and the hub touches all of them.

name: An even wheel
why: ['colouring']: the rim of 6 alternates two colours and the hub takes the third.

name: The Petersen graph
why: ['colouring']: this famous graph of 10 vertices needs exactly three colours.

name: A path with no edges at one end
why: ['colouring']. Vertices 3 and 4 have no edges, but they still need a colour: every vertex needs its clause 'at least one colour'.

name: 300 vertices
expect: ['planted colouring passes', 'clashes caught', 'missing colours caught', True]
expr: colour_cnf_report(args[0], args[1], colouring_formula(args[0], list(args[1])), [v % 3 for v in range(300)])
show: 300 vertices and about 800 random edges, made so that a colouring exists
why: Four facts are checked: a proper colouring satisfies every clause, giving two neighbours one colour breaks a clause, a vertex with no colour breaks a clause, and there are at most 4n + 3E clauses. If this test runs out of time, the formula is probably built by solving the colouring first: trying every colouring of 300 vertices is 3³⁰⁰ tries (300 threes multiplied together). Write the clauses straight from the vertices and edges instead.

name: 3,000 vertices
expect: ['planted colouring passes', 'clashes caught', 'missing colours caught', True]
expr: colour_cnf_report(args[0], args[1], colouring_formula(args[0], list(args[1])), [v % 3 for v in range(3000)])
show: 3,000 vertices and about 9,000 random edges, made so that a colouring exists
why: The same four facts. Solving the colouring yourself and writing the answer as a formula cannot work here: the reduction must not depend on the answer.
